title: Collective Symmetry and Criticality from Single-Component Fluctuations
authors: Chunhao Guo, Zhe Wang, Zheng Yan
abstract: Symmetry plays a fundamental role in modern physics by guiding the classification of phases and the construction of effective theories of critical systems. Identifying collective symmetry remains challenging because tests based on preselected order parameters can overlook hidden components. A central goal is therefore to extract symmetry and critical information from a single accessible component. We pursue this goal using Lee--Yang zero ratios generated by a single ordering field. Unmeasured components shape the projected fluctuation distribution and hence the relative zero positions. Deep in a phase with spontaneous symmetry breaking, we show analytically that the zero ratios for an isotropic order parameter approach a parameter-free Bessel sequence fixed by the number of collective components. Near quantum criticality, fluctuations deform this distribution. The resulting ratio deviations and their finite-size coupling dependence carry additional critical information. We demonstrate these results with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations of many-body systems with conventional and enlarged continuous symmetries. This approach provides quantitative access to collective symmetry and criticality without measuring every competing order.
summary: This work introduces a novel diagnostic tool using Lee-Yang zero ratios derived from single-component fluctuations to probe the full collective symmetry of quantum critical systems. By comparing these ratios to theoretical Bessel sequences, the authors can extract quantitative information about hidden symmetries and critical exponents in models like quantum magnets. This method offers a powerful way to test symmetry hypotheses without needing to measure every competing order parameter.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of identifying the full 'collective symmetry' and characterizing critical behavior in many-body systems when multiple competing orders are present.
main_result: The authors show that Lee-Yang zero ratios derived from a single accessible order parameter can quantitatively probe the underlying collective symmetry and reveal critical information by comparing deviations from a theoretical Bessel sequence benchmark.
method: The core method involves analyzing the relative positions of Lee-Yang zeros generated by a single ordering field, which are then compared against theoretical Bessel sequences fixed by the number of collective symmetry components.
model_or_system: The study applies this method to general many-body systems exhibiting continuous transitions, using specific examples like spin-1/2 square-lattice antiferromagnets with competing Néel and Valence-Bond-Solid (VBS) orders.
key_observables: Lee-Yang zero ratios ($R_{k1}$), Bessel sequence fixed by the number of components, and ratio deviations near quantum criticality.
important_parameters:
The number of collective components ($n$), the coupling constants defining competing orders (e.g., $J_w, J_s, Q$), and finite-size scaling parameters ($
u_{LY}, 
u_t$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the zero ratios are sensitive to unmeasured components, and the analysis relies on comparing results across different polynomial fitting degrees to ensure robustness.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the S4 phase cancellation and show finite-size collapses of the zero ratios ($R_{21}, R_{31}$) against theoretical Bessel ratios for various candidate symmetries ($O(3), O(4), O(5)$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework using Lee-Yang zeros, applies it to specific quantum magnetic models (e.g., CBJQ, J-Q2), and then performs detailed numerical simulations and finite-size scaling analyses to compare results across different symmetry assumptions.
why_interesting: The technique provides a powerful, non-standard diagnostic tool for characterizing critical points and emergent symmetries in strongly interacting quantum matter, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum phase transitions in AMO systems.
